slides.notes: Now, let's move on to Memory Management Techniques. As multiple processes execute simultaneously, the operating system must decide how memory is allocated, used, and managed efficiently. These techniques help ensure that each process gets the memory it needs while preventing interference between processes. As a result, the system achieves better performance, improved memory utilization, and stronger protection of memory resources.

slides.title: Memory Management Techniques
slides.body:
Contiguous vs Non-Contiguous Allocation
Heading: Memory Management Techniques
Sub-heading: Contiguous vs Non-Contiguous Allocation
slides.notes: Let's compare these two memory allocation techniques. In Contiguous Allocation, a process is stored in one continuous block of memory, making address translation straightforward. In Non-Contiguous Allocation, a process is divided across multiple memory locations, so the MMU uses mapping tables to locate each part. Another major difference is fragmentation. Contiguous Allocation is more prone to fragmentation, whereas Non-Contiguous Allocation, especially Paging, significantly reduces this problem and makes memory utilization more efficient.
tables: Each process is allocated one single, continuous block of memory
A process can occupy multiple, scattered (non-adjacent) blocks of memory
Needs a mapping table (page table / segment table) looked up by the MMU
Suffers both internal (fixed partitioning) and external (dynamic partitioning) fragmentation
Largely eliminates external fragmentation (paging); segmentation alone can still see it

slides.notes: Let's see how memory changes as processes are completed and new ones arrive. Initially, P1, P2, and P3 occupy contiguous memory blocks. When P1 finishes, its memory becomes free. Later, P4 and P5 are allocated in that available space. As the execution continues, P4 also completes, freeing its memory, while P5 continues running. slides.title: A) Contiguous Memory Allocation
slides.body:
I. Single Contiguous Allocation
One of the oldest memory management techniques
Divides memory into two partitions: one for the OS and one for user processes
Simple but leads to memory waste
Largely impractical for modern systems, though foundational for advanced techniques
slides.notes: Now, let's begin with Single Contiguous Allocation, one of the earliest memory management techniques. In this approach, the main memory is divided into two partitions—one reserved for the Operating System and the other for user processes. While this design is simple to implement, it often leaves a significant portion of memory unused, resulting in memory waste. Although it is no longer practical for modern operating systems, it provides the foundation for understanding more advanced memory allocation techniques.

slides.title: A) Contiguous Memory Allocation
slides.body:
II. Multiple Partitioning
Divides memory into separate partitions for multiple processes
Supports concurrent execution of processes
Can be implemented with Fixed Partitioning or Dynamic Partitioning
Offers more flexibility than single contiguous allocation
slides.notes: Moving on, Multiple Partitioning improves upon Single Contiguous Allocation by dividing the main memory into multiple partitions, allowing several processes to reside in memory at the same time. This enables the operating system to support the concurrent execution of processes and utilize memory more efficiently. Depending on how these partitions are created, this technique can be implemented using Fixed Partitioning or Dynamic Partitioning, both of which we'll explore next.

slides.notes: In Fixed Partitioning, the operating system divides the memory into a fixed number of partitions when the system starts, and these partition sizes remain unchanged during execution. As shown in the diagram, the processes P1, P2, and P3 are first placed in the input queue. Each process is then assigned to a 5 MB partition in main memory, even if it requires less space. The remaining portion of that partition cannot be used by another process, which leads to Internal Fragmentation.

1. Fixed Partitioning
slides.notes: Now, let's look at the advantages of Fixed Partitioning. Since the memory partitions are created in advance and remain unchanged, the operating system can allocate processes quickly without making complex allocation decisions. It is also simple and easy to manage, because the operating system doesn't have to continuously keep track of different-sized free memory spaces or update memory allocation information during execution.

slides.title: II. Multiple Partitioning
slides.body:
Disadvantage

Limits on multiprogramming, number of partitions fixes the max processes
1. Fixed Partitioning
slides.notes: Now, let's look at the disadvantages of Fixed Partitioning. One major issue is Internal Fragmentation, where part of an allocated partition remains unused if the process doesn't require all of its space, leading to wasted memory. Another limitation is that the number of partitions determines the maximum number of processes that can stay in memory at the same time. Once all partitions are occupied, additional processes have to wait, even if processor time is available.

slides.title: II. Multiple Partitioning
slides.body:
2. Dynamic Partitioning 
Also known as (Variable Allocation), here Memory is divided dynamically at runtime based on process size, a partition is created exactly matching the process’s memory requirement

slides.notes: Unlike Fixed Partitioning, this approach creates memory space only when a process arrives. Instead of assigning a fixed-size partition, the operating system allocates just enough memory to meet the process's requirement. As shown in the diagram, P1 receives 3 MB, P2 gets 1 MB, and P3 is allocated 4 MB, leaving the remaining memory available for future processes. Since each process receives only the space it needs, unused memory within a partition is minimized.

slides.title: II. Multiple Partitioning
slides.body:
2. Dynamic Partitioning 
Advantages
Partition size matches exactly the process’s need → reduces internal fragmentation
More flexible supports variable sized processes without predefined partitioning
slides.notes: Moving on, let's look at the advantages of Dynamic Partitioning. Since each partition is created to exactly match the process's memory requirement, it significantly reduces Internal Fragmentation by avoiding unused space within an allocated partition. It is also more flexible, as the operating system can allocate memory for variable-sized processes without relying on predefined fixed partitions.

slides.title: II. Multiple Partitioning
slides.body:
2. Dynamic Partitioning 
External Fragmentation — memory scattered into unusable holes over time
Allocation becomes more complex (search for holes, track free space)
Disadvantage
slides.notes: Next, Dynamic Partitioning also has a few limitations. Over time, as processes are loaded and removed, the free memory becomes scattered into small unused gaps, a problem known as External Fragmentation. Although the total free memory may be sufficient, it may not exist as one continuous block for a new process. In addition, memory allocation becomes more complex because the operating system must continuously search for suitable free spaces and keep track of the available memory.

slides.title: Fragmentation
slides.body: Fragmentation
slides.notes: Now we will be learning about the Fragmentation

slides.title: Fragmentation
slides.body:
What is Fragmentation?
Fragmentation is wasted memory that occurs while allocating memory to processes — it reduces how much of the total free memory is actually usable
Two types occur, depending on the partitioning technique used:
Internal Fragmentation
Happens with Fixed Partitioning
External Fragmentation
Happens with Dynamic Partitioning
slides.notes: Now, whenever memory is allocated and released repeatedly, some portions of memory can no longer be utilized effectively. This condition is known as Fragmentation. Although the system may still have free memory available, not all of it can be used efficiently for new processes. Based on the memory allocation technique, Fragmentation is classified into Internal Fragmentation, which occurs in Fixed Partitioning, and External Fragmentation, which occurs in Dynamic Partitioning.

slides.title: Fragmentation
slides.body:
Internal fragmentation occurs when allocated partition size is larger than the memory required by the process, leaving unused space inside the partition

Assigned space

Internal Fragmentation
1. Internal Fragmentation
slides.notes: Internal Fragmentation occurs when a process is allocated more memory than it actually requires. The extra space cannot be assigned to another process, so it remains unused. As shown in the diagram, each process occupies only a portion of its allocated partition, while the remaining area, labeled as Fragment, represents the wasted memory inside the partition.

slides.title: Internal Fragmentation
slides.body: Analogy
slides.notes: Let's understand Internal Fragmentation with a simple analogy. Imagine booking a large room but using only a small corner of it. Even though you've paid for the entire room, the remaining space cannot be used by someone else, so it goes to waste. Similarly, in Internal Fragmentation, a process is allocated a larger memory partition than it actually needs, leaving the unused space inside the allocated partition wasted.

slides.notes: External Fragmentation occurs when the available memory is broken into several small free spaces instead of one continuous block. Although the total free memory may be sufficient, a large process still cannot be allocated because it requires one contiguous block. As shown in the diagram, the free memory is scattered into 40 KB, 10 KB, and 5 KB fragments between allocated processes, making it difficult to accommodate a larger process.

slides.title: Multiple Partitioning
slides.body:
2. Dynamic Partitioning — Compaction
Compaction is a technique that solves external fragmentation by relocating all occupied memory blocks 
So that they sit next to each other, combining all scattered free space into one large contiguous block
Occupied memory blocks 
Unoccupied memory blocks
slides.notes: Now, to overcome External Fragmentation, the operating system uses a technique called Compaction. In this process, all the occupied memory blocks are moved so that they are placed next to one another. This brings together the scattered unoccupied memory blocks, creating one large contiguous block of free memory. As a result, larger processes can be allocated memory more easily.

slides.title: Multiple Partitioning
slides.body:
2. Dynamic Partitioning — Compaction
Shuffles processes toward one end of memory
Requires dynamic relocation — the base register of each process must be updated at run time as it moves
Comes with overhead: CPU time is spent copying process data during the shuffle
Only possible when relocation is dynamic (not usable with compile-time/load-time binding)
slides.notes: Next, after creating one large free memory block, the operating system has to physically move the processes so they are grouped together at one end of memory. Because each process changes its memory location, the operating system must update its base register while the process is running, a mechanism known as dynamic relocation. This movement is not free—it consumes CPU time because process data has to be copied from one location to another. For this reason, Compaction can only be performed in systems that support dynamic relocation and is not possible when addresses are fixed during compile-time or load-time binding.

slides.title: Multiple Partitioning
slides.body: Analogy
slides.notes: Let's understand Compaction with a simple analogy. Imagine a room where furniture is scattered, leaving several small empty spaces that are too small for a new sofa. By moving the existing furniture to one side, all the small gaps combine into one large empty space where the sofa can easily fit. Similarly, in Compaction, the operating system moves processes closer together, combining scattered free memory into one large contiguous block, making it easier to allocate memory to larger processes.

slides.body:
Eliminates external fragmentation

slides.notes: Finally, Compaction helps eliminate External Fragmentation by combining scattered free memory into one large contiguous block. However, this comes at a cost. The operating system must spend time moving processes in memory, and those processes are temporarily paused until the movement is complete.

slides.title: Allocation Strategies
slides.body: Allocation Strategies
slides.notes: Now we will be learn about Allocation Strategies

slides.title: Contiguous Memory Allocation
slides.body:
Allocation Schemes 
When a process needs memory, OS searches free “holes” (free blocks) and picks one using a strategy
slides.notes: Moving on, when a process requests memory, the operating system searches the available free holes, or unused memory blocks, to find a suitable location. The selection depends on the allocation scheme being used. First Fit allocates the first free hole that is large enough, Best Fit chooses the smallest suitable hole to reduce unused space, Worst Fit selects the largest available hole, and Next Fit works like First Fit but continues searching from the location of the previous allocation instead of starting from the beginning.

slides.body:

slides.notes: Let's now look at the complete allocation example. The processes arrive in the order P1, P2, P3, and P4, requesting 212 KB, 417 KB, 112 KB, and 426 KB, respectively. The operating system must allocate these processes using the available memory holes H1 to H5, shown in the diagram. We'll now see how different allocation strategies choose different holes for the same set of requests.

slides.title: Contiguous Memory Allocation
slides.body: Allocation Strategies — First Fit
slides.notes: Let's apply the First Fit strategy. Here, the operating system scans the memory from the beginning for every incoming process and selects the first hole that is large enough. So, P1 is allocated to H2, P2 is allocated to H5, and P3 fits into the remaining space of H2. When P4 arrives, none of the available holes are large enough to accommodate 426 KB, so P4 has to wait until sufficient contiguous memory becomes available.

H5 (600 KB) — first hole ≥417 KB found scanning from start
H2's leftover (288 KB) — first hole ≥112 KB found scanning from start
No hole fits (100, 176, 200, 300, 183 all < 426) → P4 waits

slides.title: Contiguous Memory Allocation
slides.body:
First Fit scans from the beginning of memory every time and takes the first hole that's big enough
Allocation Strategies — First Fit
Fast, but can leave many small unusable leftovers near the start

slides.notes: First Fit always starts searching from the beginning of memory and allocates the first hole that is large enough for the process. As shown in the diagram, it checks the holes in order until it finds a suitable one. This makes the allocation process simple and fast. However, over time, it can leave many small unused holes near the beginning of memory, reducing the chances of accommodating larger processes later.

slides.title: Contiguous Memory Allocation
slides.body: Allocation Strategies — Best Fit
slides.notes: Now, let's apply the Best Fit strategy. Unlike First Fit, the operating system checks all available holes and selects the smallest hole that can accommodate the process. As a result, P1 is allocated to H4, P2 to H2, P3 to H3, and P4 to H5. By choosing the closest-sized hole each time, Best Fit minimizes the unused space left after each allocation.
tables: H4 (300 KB) — smallest hole that still fits
H5 (600 KB) — only hole left ≥426 KB

slides.title: Contiguous Memory Allocation
slides.body:
All 4 processes get allocated — Best Fit minimizes wasted space per allocation, so it succeeds here where First Fit failed
Allocation Strategies — Best Fit
Main Memory

Best Fit
slides.notes: This example highlights the advantage of Best Fit. Since it always chooses the smallest suitable hole, memory is utilized more efficiently. As shown in the diagram, all four processes—P1, P2, P3, and P4—are allocated successfully. In this case, Best Fit succeeds where First Fit could not, because it leaves behind more useful free memory for future allocations.

slides.title: Allocation Strategies — Best Fit
slides.body:
Trade-off:
Must search all holes every time (slower), and 
Tends to create many tiny, useless leftover holes
slides.notes: However, Best Fit also has its limitations. Since the operating system must examine all the available free holes before making a decision, the allocation process is slower than First Fit. In addition, repeatedly choosing the smallest suitable hole often leaves behind many tiny free holes that are too small to be used effectively for future memory allocations.

slides.title: Contiguous Memory Allocation
slides.body: Allocation Strategies — Worst Fit
slides.notes: Now, let's apply the Worst Fit strategy. Here, the operating system always allocates the largest available hole to the incoming process. As a result, P1 is allocated to H5, P2 to H2, and P3 is placed in the remaining space of H5. However, when P4 requests 426 KB, no hole of sufficient size remains, so P4 has to wait. This shows that choosing the largest hole first does not always lead to better memory utilization.
tables: H5's leftover (388 KB) — largest hole available
No hole ≥426 KB left (100, 83, 200, 300, 276) → P4 waits

slides.title: Contiguous Memory Allocation
slides.body:
Allocation Strategies — Worst Fit
Worst Fit always picks the largest hole, gambling that the leftover stays big enough to be useful
In practice it performs similarly to or worse than First Fit and is rarely used in real systems

slides.notes: Worst Fit follows a different approach by always selecting the largest available hole for allocation. The idea is to leave behind a relatively large free space that can still be useful for future requests. As shown in the diagram, the operating system keeps choosing the largest hole in memory. However, in practice, this strategy often performs no better than First Fit and is rarely used because it does not consistently improve memory utilization.

slides.title: Contiguous Memory Allocation
slides.body: Allocation Strategies — Next Fit
slides.notes: Now, let's apply the Next Fit strategy. Similar to First Fit, it allocates the first suitable hole, but instead of restarting the search from the beginning each time, it continues from where the previous allocation ended. In this example, P1 is allocated to H2, P2 to H5, and P3 is placed in the remaining space of H2. When P4 arrives, no suitable hole is found while continuing the search, so P4 has to wait.
tables: H5 (600 KB) — scanning forward from H3
H2's leftover (288 KB) — scanning forward from H1
No hole fits scanning forward from H3 → P4 waits

slides.title: Contiguous Memory Allocation
slides.body:
Allocation Strategies — Next Fit
Next Fit behaves like First Fit but never restarts the search from the beginning 
It continues from where the last allocation left off, wrapping around when it reaches the end of memory
Main Memory

slides.notes: Next Fit is an extension of First Fit. Instead of starting the search from the beginning for every new process, it continues searching from the point where the previous allocation was made. If it reaches the end of memory without finding a suitable hole, it wraps around and continues searching from the beginning. This reduces repeated scanning of the same memory locations and can make allocation more efficient than First Fit in some cases.

slides.title: Contiguous Memory Allocation
slides.body:
Allocation Strategies — Next Fit
Usually faster than First Fit on average, since it doesn't repeatedly rescan memory it already knows is full
slides.notes: One advantage of Next Fit is that it avoids repeatedly checking the same memory locations. Since the search resumes from the previous allocation point, it often spends less time searching for a suitable hole than First Fit. As a result, Next Fit is generally faster on average, especially when memory contains many occupied blocks.

slides.title: Contiguous Memory Allocation
slides.body:
Allocation Strategies — Comparison
Heading: Contiguous Memory Allocation Sub-heading: Allocation Strategies — Comparison
slides.notes: Let's summarize the four allocation strategies. In our example, Best Fit was the only strategy that successfully allocated all four processes, while First Fit, Worst Fit, and Next Fit could allocate only three. First Fit and Next Fit are generally faster because they perform less searching, whereas Best Fit and Worst Fit take longer since they examine more memory holes before making a decision. Each strategy also creates fragmentation differently, so the most suitable choice depends on the system's performance and memory utilization requirements.
tables: Leaves small, unusable leftovers near the start
Similar to First Fit, spread more evenly

slides.title: Contiguous Memory Allocation
slides.body:
KeyNote
No single strategy is best in every case — Best Fit wastes less space per allocation but is slower and fragments memory into unusable slivers over time
Allocation Strategies — First Fit
slides.notes: Before we move on, it's important to remember that no single allocation strategy is ideal for every situation. While Best Fit reduces unused space during each allocation, it takes more time because it searches all available holes. Over time, it can also create many small, unusable free memory blocks, making future memory allocation less efficient.

slides.title: Contiguous Memory Allocation
slides.body:
Why Contiguous Allocation?
Simple to implement and control good for small systems or embedded systems
Less overhead compared to non-contiguous schemes (no paging tables)
Predictable memory layout (useful for real-time or performance-sensitive tasks)
But as process creation/deletion continues → fragmentation grows → non-contiguous schemes (paging/segmentation) are usually preferred
slides.notes: Finally, let's understand why Contiguous Memory Allocation was widely used. It is simple to implement and manage, making it suitable for small or embedded systems. Since memory is allocated as one continuous block, it also has less overhead because there is no need to maintain page tables. Another advantage is its predictable memory layout, which is useful for real-time and performance-sensitive applications. However, as processes are repeatedly created and removed, fragmentation gradually increases. Because of this limitation, modern operating systems generally prefer non-contiguous memory allocation techniques, such as Paging and Segmentation.

slides.title: Overlays
slides.body: Overlays
slides.notes: Next we will be learning about the Overlays

slides.title: Contiguous Memory Allocation
slides.body:
What are Overlays?
1
A memory management technique used to run programs larger than the available memory.
2
Divides a program into smaller sections or overlays, which       are loaded into memory only as needed.
3
Ensures that only the necessary parts of the program are in memory at any given time, optimizing memory usage.
slides.notes: Moving on, consider a situation where a program is larger than the available main memory. In such cases, loading the entire program at once is simply not possible. To overcome this limitation, the program is organized into overlays, where different parts of the program are brought into memory only when they are actually needed for execution. As the execution progresses, one overlay can replace another, so only the required portion of the program occupies memory at any given time. This allows even large programs to execute successfully while making efficient use of the limited available memory.

slides.title: Overlay
slides.body:
Overlay
Analogy
slides.notes: Let's understand Overlays with a simple analogy. Imagine borrowing books from a library with limited space on your study table. Instead of bringing all the books at once, you take only the book you need, read it, return it, and then bring the next one. Similarly, Overlays load only the required part of a program into memory. Once that part finishes execution, it is removed, and the next required part is loaded, allowing large programs to run even when memory is limited.

slides.title: Contiguous Memory Allocation
slides.body:
How Overlays work?
The program is divided into modules or overlays             (e.g., functions or parts of the program).
One overlay is loaded into memory at a time while others stay in disk storage.
Once an overlay completes its task, it is unloaded, and the next overlay is loaded, making efficient use of memory.
slides.notes: Let's understand how Overlays work. First, a large program is divided into smaller modules called overlays. Initially, only the overlay required for the current task is loaded into memory, while the remaining overlays stay on the disk. Once that overlay finishes execution, it is unloaded, and the next required overlay is loaded. This process continues until the entire program executes, allowing large programs to run efficiently even with limited memory.

Without overlays, all four program modules—Read(), Funct1(), Funct2(), and Display()—must remain in memory together, requiring 140 KB. With overlays, Read() and Display() stay in memory, while Funct1() and Funct2() are treated as overlays because they are not needed at the same time. As shown, Overlay A is loaded first, and once it finishes, it is replaced by Overlay B. This reduces the memory requirement from 140 KB to just 90 KB.

slides.title: Overlays: Example
slides.body:
Process of using Overlays
Load Overlay
Execute
Swap Overlay
slides.notes: The execution of overlays follows three simple steps. First, the required overlay is loaded from disk into memory. The CPU then executes the instructions in that overlay. Once its task is complete, the current overlay is removed, and the next required overlay is loaded into the same memory space. This cycle repeats until the entire program has finished executing.

slides.title: Process of using overlays
slides.body:
Load Overlay
The required part of the program (overlay) is loaded into memory from disk storage. Only the necessary module for the current task is brought into memory, saving space.
slides.notes: Let's begin with the first step, which is loading an overlay. When the program starts or requires a new functionality, the operating system identifies the specific overlay needed for that stage of execution and loads it from disk storage into the available main memory. Instead of bringing the entire program into memory, only this required module is loaded. This approach conserves memory, leaving the remaining space available for other processes or future overlays.

slides.title: Process of using overlays
slides.body:
Execute
The CPU executes the instructions in the loaded overlay. The overlay is active in memory and performs its task, such as running a function or processing data.
slides.notes: After the overlay is loaded, the execution phase begins. The CPU starts processing the instructions present in that overlay, allowing it to perform the specific task it was loaded for. Depending on the program, this could involve executing a function, processing data, or carrying out a particular operation. During this stage, the overlay remains in main memory until its execution is complete.

slides.title: Process of using overlays
slides.body:
Swap Overlay
Once the task is complete, the current overlay is unloaded, and the next required overlay is loaded into memory. This ensures that only the parts of the program needed at that moment are in memory.
slides.notes: Finally, once the current overlay finishes its execution, it is no longer required in memory. At this point, the operating system removes that overlay and brings in the next one needed for the program's execution. This replacement process continues throughout the program, ensuring that main memory contains only the portion of the program that is actively being used. As a result, large programs can run efficiently even when the available memory is limited.

slides.title: Overlays
slides.body:
Advantages
Advantages
Memory Efficiency: Enables large programs to run in systems with limited memory by loading only the required parts.
Reduced Memory Footprint: By loading only needed overlays,   overall memory usage is reduced, allowing more programs to  run simultaneously.
Simplicity: The overlay technique is relatively simple to   implement and doesn’t require complex algorithms.
slides.notes: Overlays offer several advantages. Since only the required part of a program is loaded into memory, even large programs can run on systems with limited memory. This also reduces the overall memory usage, allowing the operating system to accommodate more programs simultaneously. Another advantage is that the overlay technique is relatively straightforward to implement and does not require complex memory management mechanisms.

slides.title: Overlays
slides.body:
Disadvantages
Increased Overhead: Constantly swapping overlays in and out of memory can decrease performance.
Complex Program Design: Requires careful planning of how 
           the program is divided into overlays and when each part is   
           Loaded
           Limited Flexibility: Overlays are less flexible compared to 
           modern techniques like paging and segmentation, which 
           offer more dynamic memory allocation.
Disadvantage
slides.notes: Despite its benefits, overlays also have some limitations. Frequently loading and unloading overlays from disk adds extra execution time, which can reduce performance. In addition, developers must carefully decide how to divide the program into overlays and determine the correct loading sequence. Because of these limitations, overlays are less flexible than modern memory management techniques such as Paging and Segmentation, which handle memory allocation more dynamically.
